reviewerOrPass: Worker A, same AI, separate source-first pass
method: Same AI, separate source-first pass after freezing. Started with the study guide’s compulsory tables, period and prerequisite rules and individual elective descriptions, checked the four selected periods, then reassessed the workbook contributions for argument, mind, historical interpretation and normative political thought. Rechecked all three resulting schedules and the limited positive alignments.
findings: Sections 6.5–6.8 of the 2026–2027 guide give eight first-year units of 7.5 EC, eight second-year units of 7 EC plus 1, 2 and 1 EC skills units, and a third year of 30 EC minor, 20 EC advanced electives and 10 EC thesis with course. The nominal full-time Philosophy degree is Dutch-taught, with English advanced electives available. It is distinct from Philosophy of a Specific Discipline. The guide treats its elective areas as disciplinary groupings rather than formal routes.

The first year provides history and foundational philosophical subdisciplines. Completion of the first year precedes the normal second-year advanced work, the minor and the selected Year 3 electives. The 30 EC autumn minor may be a permitted minor outside Philosophy, two 15 EC minors, an approved self-designed package or eligible study abroad. Thesis writing requires the completed first and second years, and the accompanying course and thesis count once. The published normal plan reserves 15 EC electives in period 3 and 5 EC in period 4. Applying source order within those slots, choose Heidegger, Democratic Theory and Complicity in period 3, and Medieval and Early Modern Metaphysics in period 4. This avoids putting three electives into the same autumn as the minor, and preserves the order rule independently of UCR fit.

The broad option keeps the disciplinary core of introduction, ethics, mind, emotion, and free will, with political philosophy, formal logic, argument and interpretive courses. The additional options retain a philosophical core and diverge in their primary questions and methods. The ethics option studies political authority and responsibility through law, human rights, institutions and collective action. The theoretical option studies consciousness, identity, agency and meaning through mind, logic, psycholinguistics and empirical and computational approaches. In the current workbook the two cases of legal and rhetorical course timing are fixed by swapping Criminal Law with Modern Sociology and Rhetoric in Action with Perspectives on Literary Meaning. Brain and Behavior in the first autumn precedes Psycholinguistics in its only planned spring, swapped with Neurobiology. No course selection changes. Description-only Perspectives on Literary Meaning gives real interpretive practice and an independent project but does not teach the comparator’s global philosophical hermeneutics. Description-only Perception and Action supplies empirical study of perception and action and complements philosophy of mind. History of Philosophy was tested through the five philosophy courses and the historical, heritage and interpretive palette. It is a coherent direction with substantial overlap with the broad response. Three options already occupy the permitted slots. The eight original comparisons were reconsidered, with seven positive pairings retained. European Union Politics concerns institutions and empirical legislative research and is no longer equated with advanced political philosophy. Dedicated epistemology, philosophy of science and advanced historical courses remain visible gaps.
